title: Uncensored LLMs in agent loops: 31 models, 5 tasks, most fail half the time
content:
Uncensored models are mostly sold on what they will say. We wanted to know what they do: give them tools and a multi-step job, and see whether they finish, go in circles, or fall over. We ran all 31 ranked models on the Open Uncensored API through the same five agent tasks (edit a file, browse pages, multi-step math with a calculator, debug code until tests pass, analyse data), each capped at 14 turns.
Smarter originals finish more, but most still fail half the time
The intelligence of the model an uncensored edit came from does predict agent reliability: the correlation between the two is 0.56 across 31 models. Models built on originals scoring 60 or more finished 38% of tasks on average; the rest finished 27%.
Neither number is good. Even the strong group fails more often than it succeeds.
Weaker models get stuck in loops
How they fail differs too:
A loop is the model repeating the same tool call three times without progress. A crash is a malformed tool call, a made-up tool result, or giving up on tools mid-task. Models built on weaker originals loop almost twice as often. Crashes are common in both groups, so a strong original does not make a model safe to leave unattended.
The models that looped most:
- Qwen 3.8 27B Uncensored Fast by Heabsy: looped on 60% of tasks
- Qwen3.8 27B Uncensored (Aggressive): looped on 60% of tasks
- Qwen3.5 27B Queen Derestricted: looped on 60% of tasks
- Qwen3.5 27B BlueStar v3 Derestricted: looped on 60% of tasks
- Qwen3.5 27B Blossom V6.4 Derestricted: looped on 60% of tasks
If you run an agent on one of these, cap the turns and detect repeated calls.
Same original, different edits
Several originals have more than one uncensored version on the API. Tasks finished out of 5:
So far the versions of one original land within a task of each other. With one run per task that gap is noise, so we cannot yet say whether abliteration, heretic edits or fine tunes cost tool use differently. More trials will tell.
Caveats
These are early numbers: one run per task, five tasks per model, so a single task is 20 points and small differences are noise. Tool calls are written in a text format rather than native function calling, which is harder on some models than others. We will add more trials and native tool calling, and update this post when we do. The live numbers are always on the rankings page.
Try any of them in a minute
No account and no sign up. Buy a prepaid key at openuncensored.com/credits, or hand your agent openuncensored.com/agents.md and let it get one for you. Then:
curl https://openuncensored.com/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OU_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-uncensored", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'
The full, always current table is on the rankings page.

report.summary: 31 uncensored LLMs were tested on five multi-step agent tasks; even the strongest finished only 38%, with weaker models looping on repeated tool calls.
report.background: Uncensored models — usually abliterated, 'heretic'-edited, or fine-tuned variants of open-weight bases like Qwen and DeepSeek — are marketed almost entirely on what they will say, i.e. whether they comply with requests that aligned models refuse. That made refusal rate the de facto benchmark for the category. But a growing share of real usage puts models inside agent loops, where a model must call tools, read results, and iterate toward a goal over many turns. That setting stresses different failure modes: instruction-following under long context, structured output discipline, error recovery, and the ability to notice it is stuck. Open Uncensored runs an API and public rankings for these models, and this experiment is an early attempt to measure agentic reliability rather than compliance, since buyers increasingly pick uncensored models to run unattended automation rather than chat.
key_points: The test was uniform: all 31 ranked models on the Open Uncensored API ran the same five agent tasks — edit a file, browse pages, multi-step math with a calculator, debug code until tests pass, and analyse data — each capped at 14 turns. Tool calls were written in a text format rather than native function calling, which the authors note is harder on some models than others.

Base-model intelligence does predict agent reliability, but weakly: the correlation is 0.56. Models built on originals scoring 60+ finished 38% of tasks on average, versus 27% for the rest. Neither number is usable — even the strong group fails more often than it succeeds when left to run a multi-step job.

Failure modes split into loops and crashes. A loop is the model repeating the same tool call three times without progress; a crash is a malformed tool call, a fabricated tool result, or abandoning tools mid-task. Weaker-based models loop almost twice as often, but crashes are common in both groups — so a strong original does not make a model safe to leave unattended.

Looping is concentrated and dramatic: five 27B models — Heabsy's Qwen 3.8 27B Uncensored Fast, Qwen3.8 27B Uncensored (Aggressive), and the Qwen3.5 27B Queen, BlueStar v3 and Blossom V6.4 derestricted builds — each looped on 60% of tasks. Any agent running these should hard-cap turns and detect repeated identical calls.

Where one original has several uncensored versions on the API, they finished within one task of each other. With one run per task, that gap is noise, so the data cannot yet say whether abliteration, heretic edits or fine-tuning damage tool use differently. The authors flag the sample as early: five tasks per model means one task is 20 points.
report.impact: The result reframes how uncensored models should be judged. Buyers have treated refusal removal as the only axis that matters; this suggests compliance and competence are largely independent, and that an abliterated 27B can be perfectly willing to run your automation and still fail half the time. For developers, the practical takeaway is defensive engineering rather than model selection: cap turns, detect repeated identical tool calls, validate tool-call schema, and never let an uncensored model write results back unchecked. For users, it means agent products built on these models will feel unreliable rather than dangerous — spinning, inventing tool output, or silently quitting. Expect agentic leaderboards to become the real buying signal.
report.tools: Watch the live rankings at openuncensored.com and try models via a prepaid API key (openuncensored.com/credits); agents can self-onboard from openuncensored.com/agents.md. For your own harness, pair any uncensored model with loop guards: turn caps plus hash-based detection of repeated tool calls, and schema validation before execution. Tracing tools such as Langfuse, AgentOps or Braintrust make loops and malformed calls visible. If you evaluate models yourself, use Inspect AI or lm-evaluation-harness with native function calling rather than text-format tool calls.
